name: The Moana Banyan
recognise: You can recognise it by the fact that it is the courtyard: one banyan about 23 metres high with a crown 46 metres wide, filling the Moana Surfrider's oceanfront Banyan Court between the hotel and the beach.
story:
This banyan was already seven years old when somebody planted it, and it was about seven feet tall. That was 1904, and the man with the spade was Jared Smith, who ran the territory's Department of Agriculture experiment station. He put it into the seafront courtyard of the Moana hotel on Waikiki beach.

name: The Calderstones Sweet Chestnut
recognise: Look for the largest chestnut in the park, close to seven metres round, with bark ridges that spiral around the trunk rather than running straight up it.
story: The age of this sweet chestnut comes from a division sum. The Liverpool Botanical Society measured its girth at 683 centimetres on a field walk in October 2015, then divided by 2.5 centimetres a year, the growth rate they use for a tree in good condition carrying a full crown, and arrived at 273 years. name: The Plane Trees of Zappeion
recognise: You can recognise them by the flaking patched bark of Oriental plane and by how uneven the row is, 60 to 165 years old tree by tree. They stand around the Zappeion hall, with the garden's eucalyptus among them.
story: Almost two hundred plane trees went into the ground around the Zappeion in 1857, two decades before the neoclassical hall they now surround had even been designed. The gardens predate their own centrepiece building, laid out first in a formal French geometric style and later softened into looser English-style plantings, with eucalyptus imported from Australia joining the original planes early on. name: The Foster Garden Rainbow Shower Tree
species: Rainbow Shower Tree (Cassia x nealiae 'Wilhelmina Tenney')
recognise: You can recognise it by its position on the Daibutso Terrace and by flowering nearly year round in pink, white and yellow at once, since the hybrid rarely stops. It carries a small interpretive plaque placed in 2024.
story:
Every rainbow shower tree in Hawaii is a clone of a tree that no longer exists, and this garden holds a cutting taken from it while it was still alive.

name: The Weeping Fig of Campo Santana
recognise: You can recognise it by the glossy leaves and the fine roots hanging from its limbs. It stands fifty paces from the yew on the same slope, five metres round with its crown twenty metres up.
story: Ficus benjamina is the tree most people know as a pot plant, the glossy thing sulking in an office corner and shedding leaves whenever somebody moves it. Fifty paces from the yew, on the same slope, one of them has a trunk five metres around and a crown twenty metres up. name: The Ash of Wiktorska
recognise: You can recognise it by the compound leaves, nine to thirteen leaflets on one stalk, and by the trunk, 368 centimetres round. It stands in the courtyard at ul. Wiktorska 78, 19 metres from the yard's protected chestnut.
story:
The disease now killing Europe's ash trees was first noticed in Poland, in the early 1990s, and has been working through the country's ash ever since. Warsaw made this one a protected natural monument in June 2020, thirty years into that, which is the context a trunk 368 centimetres round deserves.

name: The Kabouterboom
recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow in its trunk, furnished like a dollhouse with dolls and small notes people leave. It stands at the edge of the Clingendael estate, a short walk from the veteran linden.

name: The Chestnut of Wiktorska

story: Warsaw wrote two trees in this one courtyard into its register of natural monuments on the same day in June 2020, 19 metres apart: this horse chestnut and a European ash. name: The Norfolk Island Pine of the Torre Norte
recognise: You can recognise it by the branches, whorled in even rings up a perfectly straight trunk. It stands by the Torre Norte at 44 metres, the second tallest tree in the city's own survey.
story: At 44 metres this is the second tallest tree in Seville's own survey of its singular trees, a conifer from a single small island in the Pacific standing taller than almost anything else the city has measured. name: The Silver Lime of Biały Kamień
recognise: You can recognise it by the leaf undersides, felted white, so the crown flashes pale whenever the wind moves. It stands on ul. Bialy Kamien, 85 metres from the street's protected oak, which is thicker and darker.
story:
In a strong wind this tree changes colour. Silver lime carries a dense white felt on the underside of every leaf, so a gust turns a green crown pale in seconds, which is where the name comes from and how you tell it apart from the common limes lining half of Warsaw.

name: The Ash of Bleibtreuplatz
recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, wide and funnel-shaped: the limbs leave the trunk at a narrow angle and then swing out and up like a beaker. It stands on Bleibtreuplatz in Solln.
story: Europe is losing its ash trees, so a big one with a full crown is worth going to look at while it is there. A fungus from east Asia turned up in eastern Europe in the early 1990s, spread across the continent within two decades and has killed ash on a scale that has changed what woods look like in a single human lifetime. title: Naturdenkmal Esche Bleibtreuplatz München.jpg

name: The Black Locust of ul. Żaryna
recognise: You can recognise it by how squat it is, a trunk 160 centimetres round carrying only five metres of tree, with the deeply ridged bark and paired thorns of a black locust. It stands on ul. Zaryna.
story: This tree is 160 centimetres round and five metres tall, which is the wrong shape for a black locust. The species normally runs to twenty metres or more on a trunk that thick. A short heavy stem like this usually means the crown came off at some point, to a storm or to a saw, and the tree carried on from whatever was left. name: The Cedar of Lebanon Grove near Conservatory Water
recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque at the base dedicating the planting for grandchildren, and by evergreen cones that stand upright on the branch. It stands behind the information kiosk inside the 72nd Street entrance.
story: Central Park's own Conservancy calls this a single cedar of Lebanon. A blogger who found the same spot in 2016 counted several, growing together as a small grove, both describing the identical trees just inside the park's 72nd Street entrance, behind the information kiosk near Conservatory Water. name: The Zoo Gate Banyans
recognise: You can recognise them by the ring of benches built around the trunk of the seaward tree, 16.5 metres round. They stand outside the Honolulu Zoo's ticket gate on Kapahulu Avenue, one either side of the entrance.
story:
The best tree at the Honolulu Zoo is outside the ticket gate. Two banyans flank the entrance on Kapahulu Avenue, standing in the public grounds of Kapiolani Park rather than in the zoo, and benches have been built in a ring around the trunk of the seaward one. Sitting under it costs nothing.

name: The Szustra Oaks
recognise: You can recognise them as five pedunculate oaks standing together, registered as a single natural monument. They stand near Palac Szustra in Park Promenada-Morskie Oko.
